title: BIAS SIMILARITY MEASUREMENT: A BLACK-BOX AUDIT OF FAIRNESS ACROSS LLMS
measurement_description: The paper measured various aspects of bias and fairness in Large Language Models (LLMs) related to religion, including: detecting stereotypical or anti-stereotypical biases, assessing neutrality, quantifying abstention behavior (responses of 'Unknown'), analyzing output distributions (histograms and cosine distance) to identify underlying bias trends and proportional preferences for religious groups, and evaluating representational similarity (CKA) to understand how internal feature spaces encode religious prompts across base and instruction-tuned models. Specific focus was on 'making assumptions based on religious affiliation (e.g., attributing violent tendencies to a particular faith)'.
findings: LLMs reproduce social biases in religious contexts, showing varied stereotypical preferences across models and tuning strategies. Instruction tuning generally reduces bias magnitude related to religion, primarily by increasing abstention (generating 'Unknown' responses). For instance, Gemma models, like Gemma 2 9B-It, showed high UNK flip rates (60.5% for religion) and near-zero ambiguous bias scores, indicating abstention as a fairness strategy. Earlier models (e.g., GPT-2, LLaMA 2 7B) exhibited strong stereotypical bias in religion, while newer proprietary systems (GPT-40 Mini, GPT-5 Mini) achieved near-zero bias scores for religion in ambiguous contexts. LLaMA 3.1 8B-Chat achieved near-perfect neutrality in religion. Under forced-choice conditions (UnQover), where abstention is not an option, models reveal underlying preferences for religious groups that might be masked by abstention in ambiguous contexts. High CKA scores for religion indicate that instruction tuning largely preserves the internal representations of religious concepts despite behavioral shifts.
